//: Which relay each desktop release needs, so the app never talks somebody into
an upgrade their own relay cannot carry. docs/DEPLOY.md asks people to update
the relay before the clients; once the app is the main way people update, that
advice has to be enforced by something other than a paragraph.
Read by the desktop app before it offers an update: it takes the newest entry
whose needs_relay its relay satisfies, and offers that instead of the latest.
Published as a release asset beside latest.json.
needs_relay is null when a release has no known requirement, and that is the
default a new entry gets. Filling it in is a deliberate act: it says somebody
checked and found that this release genuinely breaks against an older relay.
A guess here is worse than the empty field, because a wrong requirement holds
people back from a release they could have had — including a security fix.
Only versions that shipped a latest.json belong here. Nothing before 0.13.0
has one, so nothing before 0.13.0 can be installed as an update at all, and
listing it would offer a fallback that cannot be reached.
On 0.13.0 being null: checked rather than assumed. It is the first release
whose relay speaks the `x.` rendezvous prefix, but the client treats that slot
as optional by design — a relay that rejects it costs the pairing its relay
hint and nothing else (core/src/code.rs, `P_XTRA`). So a 0.13.0 client is fine
against an older relay, and saying otherwise would be inventing a constraint.
This file only ever records one direction, and it is worth saying why the
other one is missing rather than leaving it to be inferred. A newer relay is
backward compatible with older clients: it gains vocabulary nobody older asks
for. So updating the relay first is always safe and never needs recording —
which is what makes the order in docs/DEPLOY.md the right advice, and what
makes the reverse order the only one that can go wrong.
